title: Night gate record after the reed mat slipped
public_context: Shared irrigation channels depend on local rules for ordinary turns and urgent repairs. Committee records may describe who can alter a gate, how neighbors are notified, and what happens when water is diverted temporarily. A written incident account can settle some procedural questions while leaving later effects to another season.
source_title: Lower Bend irrigation committee incident report
source_text:
At 9:10 on 18 June, the Lower Bend ditch tender reported that a reed mat had slipped across the east culvert. Water backed against the upstream footbridge and the lower vegetable plots received only a trickle. The normal schedule gave the east branch the first evening turn, but the committee's rule allowed a temporary bypass when a culvert blockage threatened the bridge or a planted bed. The bypass had to be witnessed by one upstream and one downstream holder.

The tender called the two holders listed for that evening. Ivo arrived from the upstream terrace and Lin from the lower allotments. They agreed to open the stone relief notch for twenty minutes while the tender lifted the mat. Lin kept a lantern at the channel marker, and Ivo watched the bridge footings. The water level fell enough for the tender to pull the mat free with a hooked pole. The report records that no bank stones were removed and no tools entered the culvert.

The committee measured the notch opening with a marked slat before restoring the gate to its scheduled position. The lower plots received the remaining turn, and the next household on the branch was notified by a runner because the bell rope had snapped earlier that week. The report says the temporary release did not reach the west branch. It also states that no holder lost a scheduled turn as a penalty for the repair.

At the next morning's walk, the bridge footing was dry and the east culvert passed water without obstruction. The tender tied the recovered reed mat above the channel rather than throwing it away, since its weave was still intact. A separate note asked the committee to replace the frayed bell rope before the next rotation. The holders signed the incident report, and the clerk entered the twenty-minute bypass in the monthly water ledger.

The account credits the quick repair to the witnesses' presence, but it does not compare the repair with any other response. It gives no measurement of crop stress in the lower plots and does not say whether the committee changed the order of turns later in June. The next scheduled inspection was entered for the following Monday, when the tender planned to check the culvert after the upper terrace's usual turn.

consistency_questions.question: How did the emergency release affect the ordinary turn schedule and the west branch?
consistency_questions.reference_answer: The two witnesses allowed a twenty-minute relief-notch opening; the lower plots received the remaining scheduled turn, the release did not reach the west branch, and no holder lost a turn as a penalty.

consistency_questions.question: What evidence links the repair action to the later condition of the channel?
consistency_questions.reference_answer: The witnessed opening let the tender remove the reed mat without entering the culvert or removing bank stones. The next morning the footing was dry and water passed freely, and the event was logged.
